The example uses three packages: ausparl, dplyr for working with the results, and ggplot2 for
one chart.

```{r setup}
library(ausparl)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(ggplot2)
```

## 1. Connect and check the version

ausparl works on one database at a time, opened read-only with `db_connect()`. There are three
ways to open one:

- **The sample bundled with ausparl**: eight sitting days, nothing to download. Good for
  trying the package; the numbers are small.

  ```r
  db_connect(sample = TRUE)
  ```

- **The full database in a folder of your own**, such as `dataset/` in this repository. Download
  it once (about 9.5 GB), then open it by its path:

  ```r
  db_download(dir = "dataset")
  db_connect(path = "dataset/hansard.duckdb")
  ```

- **The full database in the default place.** `db_download()` with no `dir` installs it in your
  R user data directory, and `db_connect()` with no arguments then opens it. So does setting
  the `AUSPARL_DB` environment variable to the path of a copy you already have.

This example opens the full database if it is in `dataset/`, and the sample otherwise:

```{r connect-db}
# Quarto runs this file from example/; a plain R run starts in the top folder.
full_db <- c("dataset/hansard.duckdb", "../dataset/hansard.duckdb")
full_db <- full_db[file.exists(full_db)]
on_sample <- length(full_db) == 0
if (on_sample) {
  db_connect(sample = TRUE)
} else {
  db_connect(path = full_db[1])
}
```

```{r sample-note}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
if (on_sample) {
  cat(
    "\nThis run uses the sample database, so the numbers below are small. For the full",
    "database, run `db_download(dir = \"dataset\")` once from the top folder of the",
    "repository and run the example again.\n"
  )
}
```

`db_info()` says which build is open: quote `schema_version` and `built_at` in your methods.
`fts_available` says whether full-text search (section 3) can run.

```{r connect}
db_info() |>
  select(schema_version, built_at, n_sittings, n_actions, n_members, fts_available)
```

## 2. Find a member and their profile

Every member has a Parliamentary Handbook id, `PHID`, which links them across all tables.
`find_member()` finds it from pieces of a name, in any order and any case.

```{r find-member}
howard <- find_member("john howard")
howard |> select(PHID, DisplayName, chambers, first_service, last_service)
```

`member_profile()` gathers what is recorded about one member. A ministerial role reads as
`Role` + `Prep` + `Entity`, for example "Minister" + "for" + "Finance".

```{r profile}
profile <- member_profile(howard$PHID)
profile$ministry_records |>
  distinct(Role, Prep, Entity, RDateStart, RDateEnd) |>
  mutate(role = trimws(paste(Role, Prep, Entity))) |>
  select(role, RDateStart, RDateEnd) |>
  arrange(RDateStart)
```

## 3. A term across the years

`search_speeches_by_terms()` finds the turns that use a term, with `n_hits`, the number of
times it occurs. With `collect = FALSE` the counting by year runs inside the database.

```{r term-by-year}
if (isTRUE(db_info()$fts_available)) {
  by_year <- search_speeches_by_terms("immigration", include_text = FALSE, collect = FALSE) |>
    group_by(year = year(date)) |>
    summarise(n_turns = n(), n_mentions = sum(n_hits, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
    collect() |>
    arrange(year)
  print(
    ggplot(by_year, aes(year, n_mentions)) +
      geom_line() +
      geom_point() +
      labs(x = NULL, y = "Mentions", title = "\"immigration\" in Hansard, by year")
  )
} else {
  cat("Full-text search is not available on this machine, so the term search is skipped.\n")
}
```

## 4. Turns, interjections, government and opposition

The database keeps the structure of debate. On 15 October 2002, in the House, a turn can be
one speech broken by interjections: `get_speech_turns()` returns it as one row, with
`n_actions` the number of pieces it was recorded in. `get_interjections()` says who
interrupted whom.

```{r turns}
turns <- get_speech_turns(sitting_id = "house_2002-10-15", include_text = FALSE)
nrow(turns)
turns |>
  filter(n_actions > 1) |>
  select(turn_no, name_raw, party_at_time, n_actions) |>
  head(5)

get_interjections(from = "2002-10-15", to = "2002-10-15", chamber = "house") |>
  count(interjector_name, target_name, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(5)
```

`add_government_status()` adds whether the speaker's party was in government that day. On a
lazy table the whole count runs in the database. Here, the 40th Parliament (2002-2004).

```{r government}
get_speeches(parliament_id = 40, include_text = FALSE, collect = FALSE) |>
  filter(!is.na(PHID)) |>
  add_government_status() |>
  count(chamber, government_status_at_time) |>
  arrange(chamber, government_status_at_time) |>
  collect()
```

## 5. Hand off to text analysis

`as_corpus()` turns a result with text into a quanteda corpus; the other columns become
document variables. Here, John Howard's turns in the 40th Parliament, and their most
frequent words.

```{r corpus}
corp <- get_speeches(member = howard$PHID, parliament_id = 40, limit = 100) |>
  as_corpus()
quanteda::ndoc(corp)

quanteda::tokens(corp, remove_punct = TRUE, remove_numbers = TRUE) |>
  quanteda::tokens_tolower() |>
  quanteda::tokens_remove(quanteda::stopwords("en")) |>
  quanteda::dfm() |>
  quanteda::topfeatures(15)
```

```{r disconnect}
#| include: false
db_disconnect()
```
